extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and readers of English constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the laws, customs, and constitutional principles governing the Parliament of England/Great Britain, including its composition, privileges, powers, and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal prerogative to convoke parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: No parliament can be convened by its own authority, or by the authority of any, except the king alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: spontaneous meeting would create uncertainty as to which assembled part constituted the legislature; the king is a single person whose will is uniform and steady and capable of acting when no parliament exists. The crown alone calls parliaments and alone can dissolve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for necessity (convention parliaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of necessity (e.g., Restoration 1660; Convention of 1688), the houses have met and acted without the king's writs when the throne was vacant or extraordinary necessity existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such meetings are justifiable only on a principle of necessity; where validated, statutes (e.g., 1 W. & M. st.1 c.1; Stat. 12 Car. II c.1) were later passed to declare the proceedings good. These are narrow exceptions and cannot be treated as general precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limits on intermission and frequency of parliaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Antient statutes required annual meeting 'if need be'; later statutes (16 Car. II c.1, 6 W. & M. c.2) enacted that sitting and holding of parliaments shall not be intermitted above three years and require a new parliament within three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2 declares it a right that parliaments ought to be held frequently; the three-year limit reduces vague 'frequency' to a certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent parts of Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament consists of the king (in his royal political capacity), the lords spiritual, the lords temporal (who sit with the king in one house), and the commons (who sit separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three estates and the king together form the body politic; the king must meet them in person or by representation for a parliament to begin; consent of all three is required to make a new law binding on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must be a branch of the legislature (balance of constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power should be a branch, though not the whole, of the legislature, to prevent tyranny from either total union or total disjunction of powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical lesson: when the houses excluded royal authority they later assumed administrative power and caused oppression; the crown's legislative share (mainly rejection) preserves mutual checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown's legislative role is primarily negative (royal negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown's share of legislation consists in the power of rejecting rather than resolving; the crown cannot of itself begin alterations in the established law but may approve or disapprove alterations suggested by the two houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Roman tribunes' negative: crown prevents wrong rather than does wrong; this negative functions as a check within the mixed constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual checks among branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Each branch (people/commons, nobility/peers, and crown) acts as a check on the others: commons check the nobility, nobility check the commons, and the king checks both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two houses can inquire into, impeach, and punish the king's evil counsellors, thereby checking executive power; the mixed nature prevents separation and excessive usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lords spiritual: composition and voting practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The lords spiritual consist of two archbishops and twenty-four bishops (historically also mitred abbots); they hold baronies and sit in the House of Lords; their votes intermingle with the temporal lords and the majority of such intermixture binds both estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although legally distinct from lords temporal, in practice they are blended as 'the lords'; authorities (Selden, Coke) give instances on effect of intermixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lords temporal: composition and creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The lords temporal are the peers of the realm (dukes, marquisses, earls, viscounts, barons), sitting by descent, creation, or (for Scottish representative peers) election; their number is indefinite and may be increased by the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical debates: attempts to limit the peerage (e.g., during George I) were politically resisted; the crown's power to create peers affects the assembly's composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and necessity of a distinct nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction of rank and honours is necessary to reward public service, excite virtuous ambition, and to support the rights of crown and people by forming a barrier to encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nobility provides gradual scale of dignity and stability; if confounded with the mass, privileges would be overwhelmed by popular torrent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons: composition and representative function
rubrics_metrics.description: The commons consist of men of property not seated in the Lords; they are represented by knights (counties) and citizens/burgesses (cities/boroughs); every member, though chosen by a district, serves for the whole realm and is not strictly bound to consult constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation is for the 'common' or general interest (writ of summons language given). Practical reasons for representative government in a large state are discussed via historical analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative validity requires assent of all three parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is enacted for law by one, or by two only, of the three constituent parts is no statute and does not bind the subject (except in matters relating to their own privileges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During anarchy commons once asserted sole legislative authority, but statute 13 Car. II c.1 enacted penalties for affirming legislative authority of either house without the king (praemunire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament's sovereign and extensive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament has sovereign and uncontrollable authority to make, confirm, enlarge, restrain, abrogate, repeal, revive, and expound laws concerning matters of all denominations (ecclesiastical, temporal, civil, military, maritime, criminal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include altering succession, religion, and constitution (act of union, triennial/septennial statutes). Authorities (Coke, Montesquieu) commented on the breadth and risks of such power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age requirement for members (minimum 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: No one shall sit or vote in either house of parliament unless he be twenty-one years of age (statute 7 & 8 W. III c.25); minors were previously incapacitated by law and custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents immature delegation of supreme trust; the statute makes the rule explicit for the Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of oaths and declarations before sitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must, before voting or sitting, take oaths of allegiance, supremacy, and abjuration, and subscribe declarations against transubstantiation and invocation of saints (statutes 30 Car. II st.2 and 1 Geo. I c.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements were enacted to prevent crude innovations in religion and government and to guard against unsuitable members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aliens excluded from membership
rubrics_metrics.description: No alien, born out of the dominions of the crown of Great Britain, even if naturalized, shall be capable of being a member of either house (12 & 13 W. III c.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision intended to prevent dangers from foreign attachments, connexions, or dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lex et consuetudo parliamenti: house decides its own matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular law and custom of parliament (lex et consuetudo parliamenti) is founded on the maxim that whatever matter arises concerning either house ought to be examined, discussed, and adjudged in that house to which it relates, and not elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: lords will not suffer commons to settle peerage claims; commons will not allow lords to judge burgess elections; these maxims and methods rest within parliament and are better learned from records and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary privileges are broad and indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges of parliament are very large and indefinite; historically the principal privilege was that its privileges were not certainly known to any but the parliament itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness preserves dignity and independence against executive harassment; the high court of parliament claims to determine its own privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege of speech and debate immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of speech, debates, and proceedings in parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of parliament (statute 1 W. & M. st.2 c.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This freedom is demanded of the king by the speaker at the opening of every new parliament and protects members' speech from outside questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege of person and immunities during session
rubrics_metrics.description: Privilege of person includes immunity from illegal violence and from legal arrests, arrests of menial servants, entries on lands, distraints or seizures of goods during the session; for peers this personal privilege is perpetual, for commoners it extends forty days after prorogation and forty days before the next meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These immunities are ancient and meant to prevent diversion from public business; they do not protect against crimes of public malignity (treason, felony, breach of the peace) or cases requiring surety of the peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on privileges after dissolution or prorogation
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges which obstruct the ordinary course of justice cease immediately after dissolution or prorogation of parliament or adjournment of the houses for above a fortnight (statutes 12 W. III c.3 and 11 Geo. II c.24); members may then be sued like ordinary subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions and statutory qualifications: the king may sue for debts; a member may be sued for misdemeanour or breach of trust in public office (2 & 3 Ann. c.18); privileged traders may be served process for debts (4 Geo. III c.33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary law (lex et consuetudo) best learned from precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar law and custom of parliament is vast and better learned from the rolls of parliament, records, precedents, and continual experience than from a single exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coke's observation: this law is 'ab omnibus quaerenda, a multis ignorata, a paucis cognita'; detailed practice is derived from historical records.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords forest privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Every lord spiritual or temporal summoned to parliament, passing through the king's forests, may, both in going and returning, kill one or two of the king's deer without warrant (charter of the forest; confirmed in parliament 9 Hen. III).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antient privilege tied to the rights of lords in transit through royal forests; ceremonial conditions (in view of forester or by horn) noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance of judges and legal officers in the House of Lords
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords has the right to be attended by judges of king's bench, common pleas, barons of the exchequer of the coif, and masters of chancery for legal advice and dignity; secretaries of state and king's learned counsel formerly attended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance supports judicial advice and dignity of proceedings; regular writs of summons historically issued at each parliament's beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer proxy voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Every peer may, by licence obtained from the king, make another lord of parliament his proxy to vote for him in his absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This privilege distinguishes peers from commons members, who are representatives of constituencies and cannot be proxies for one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer's right to enter dissent/protest
rubrics_metrics.description: A peer has the right, by leave of the house, when a vote passes contrary to his sentiments, to enter his dissent on the journals of the house with reasons (styled his protest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves an official record of disagreement and the reasons for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills affecting peerage to originate in the House of Lords
rubrics_metrics.description: All bills that may in their consequences in any way affect the rights of the peerage are by custom to have their first rise and beginning in the House of Peers and to suffer no changes or amendments in the House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom preserves peerage rights by originating such measures in the Lords and preventing Commons' amendments that would affect the peerage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory regulation of election of Scottish representative peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute 6 Ann. c.23 regulates the election of the sixteen representative peers of North Britain, prescribing oaths, mode of balloting, prohibiting unusual attendance, and providing that no other matter shall be treated at that assembly but the election (on pain of praemunire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute implements union articles and confines the assembly's competence strictly to the election business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons' exclusive right to originate grants of supplies (money bills)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the ancient indisputable privilege and right of the House of Commons that all grants of subsidies or parliamentary aids begin in their house and are first bestowed by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly given reason: supplies are raised upon the body of the people; author argues true reason is constitutional (lords' permanence and susceptibility to crown influence), not that only commons are taxed.
